Cyberattack in 2021 Disrupted China’s Engineering & Construction Firms

BEIJING, June 18—A major cyberattack targeting the Engineering & Construction sector in China in mid-2021 caused widespread disruption to business operations, halting projects and delaying contract deliveries, according to industry sources and analysts. The incident, which involved ransomware infiltrating IT systems, affected several leading firms, including China Aluminum International Engineering Corp Ltd.

The attack, which began in early June 2021, was characterized by a rapid deployment of ransomware that encrypted critical project management and financial data. Local media reported that at least nine major firms were affected, with operations suspended for periods ranging from several hours to more than a week.

China Aluminum International Engineering Corp Ltd confirmed at the time that its internal systems had been compromised. In a statement released in July 2021, the company said, “We experienced a temporary suspension of certain digital platforms due to a cybersecurity incident. Immediate containment measures were implemented, and no sensitive client data was lost.” The company reported that normal operations resumed within ten days, after a coordinated response with cybersecurity experts and authorities.

A manager at another affected company, Qingdao Engineering Solutions, who declined to be named, told local press, “Our project timelines were pushed back by almost two weeks. The attack encrypted our design files and delayed procurement processes. We had to rely on manual records while systems were restored.”

The China Association of Engineering Contractors estimated that the sector lost approximately 620 million yuan (about $97 million) in revenue due to halted operations and remediation efforts. “This event highlighted vulnerabilities in the digital infrastructure of the construction industry,” said association spokesperson Li Wenhua. “While companies have made rapid advances in digitizing workflows, many have not invested sufficiently in cybersecurity.”

Analysts say the attack was among the most serious to hit the sector in recent years, exposing reliance on centralized digital platforms for project bidding, supply chain management and engineering design. “The Engineering & Construction industry in China has become highly interconnected through digital systems, making it a tempting target for ransomware actors,” noted cybersecurity consultant Zhang Yida.

In the aftermath, firms accelerated investments in cybersecurity and disaster recovery solutions. “We saw a surge in demand for security audits and staff training after the attack,” said Liu Fang, an IT executive at a Beijing-based cybersecurity firm.

By late 2021, all affected companies had restored operations and reinforced their IT defenses. Trade unions reported no long-term job losses, though some workers faced temporary furloughs.

Authorities did not disclose the perpetrators’ identities. The Ministry of Industry and Information Technology later issued new guidelines, urging Engineering & Construction firms to bolster cyber resilience and report incidents promptly.
